paragraphs: Friend, here's the big idea: the beasts look powerful, but the power is borrowed. The dragon gave the first beast his power and his throne and great authority (Revelation 13:2). Twice John says the beast was "given" something: a mouth to speak, and authority to act for 42 months (Revelation 13:5). So when the crowd asks, "Who is like the beast, and who can wage war against it?" (Revelation 13:4), the passage wants you to notice that the beast's power was handed to it.

Now the second beast. It has two horns like a lamb, but it speaks like a dragon (Revelation 13:11). It deceives with signs, and it makes buying and selling depend on a mark (Revelation 13:14, 17). Friend, something can look gentle and still be wrong, so this passage is teaching us to listen to what is being said and not just look at how pretty the packaging is. A cookie box with a beautiful bow can still have burnt cookies in it, and I have PACKED that box.

This part is heavy, so I'll say it plainly: the beast was permitted to wage war against the saints and to conquer them (Revelation 13:7). John doesn't hide that. But he says what it calls for: "Here is a call for the perseverance and faith of the saints" (Revelation 13:10). He also tells us that those whose names are written in the Book of Life belong to the Lamb who was slain (Revelation 13:8). That is why my ovens stay ready: I don't know when the Supper comes, but I know who I belong to, and I'm staying faithful until then. The story isn't over, friend, and neither is this teaching.
